body.en: The poet describes her mother with *images* of death and decay: a pale, ashen face, an open mouth while dozing, a look almost like a corpse. Outside the car she sees young trees seeming to sprint past and merry children spilling out of their homes. These lively images stand for youth, growth and the continuity of life.

Outside: happy children rushing out of homes

say.en: On the left, inside the car; on the right, outside.
She sees her mother dozing; outside, young trees seem to run past.
The mother's face is ashen; outside, children rush out joyfully.
Inside is stillness; outside is motion.
So the contrast is between the end of life and its renewal.

body.en: By turning away to the window, the poet tries to escape a painful thought. But the bright scene outside only sharpens the *contrast*: the world is young and moving, while her mother is ageing and still. The contrast makes the reader feel the passing of time.

By turning away to the window, the poet tries to escape a painful thought. But the bright scene outside only sharpens the contrast: the world is young and moving, while her mother is ageing and still. The contrast makes the reader feel the passing of time. Looking outside is an attempt to escape.
The contrast sharpens her pain.
Theme: the passage of time.

problem.en: Why does the poet look out at the young trees and merry children?

steps.en: Say what she was trying to do: escape the painful thought of her mother's ageing.
Explain the images: they show youth, energy and life.
Show the effect: the contrast only deepens her awareness of time.

answer.en: She looks outside to drive away the painful thought of her mother's age and possible death. The sprinting trees and merry children show youth and energy, and this contrast with her pale mother makes her feel the passage of time even more.
